w: William the Conqueror held his Christmas court in the chapter house here in 1085 and ordered up the Domesday Book on the spot; Henry III was crowned in the abbey the following century. Its 14th-century cloisters show the earliest fan vaulting in England, and the murdered Edward II lies in a shrine inside.
s: Where the Domesday Book was ordered into being
_facts: Originated as a minster founded around 679, became Gloucester Abbey
William the Conqueror held his Christmas Court here in 1085, ordering the Domesday Book
Henry III crowned at the abbey in 1216
14th-century cloisters show the earliest surviving fan vaulting
Contains the shrine of the murdered Edward II

w: Charles III inherited an overgrown Georgian garden here in 1980 and spent decades turning it organic, working with garden designer Rosemary Verey and naturalist Miriam Rothschild to fill it with rare trees and heirloom seeds. Now over 30,000 visitors a year tour grounds run on the King's own environmental principles.
s: The King's organic garden outside Tetbury
_facts: Family residence of King Charles III and Queen Camilla, near Tetbury
Purchased by the Duchy of Cornwall in 1980; gardens were overgrown at the time
Gardens developed with Rosemary Verey and Miriam Rothschild
Open to the public since 1996, over 30,000 visitors a year
Run on organic gardening and lawn management principles

w: Economist David Ricardo had this house rebuilt in the 1820s by architect George Basevi, though it's better known today as Princess Anne's country home since 1976. The Grade II* listed house stays firmly private, but its grounds open occasionally for a horse trial or craft fair.
_facts: Country house between Minchinhampton and Avening, originally built in the 1770s
Rebuilt from 1820 by George Basevi for economist David Ricardo
Country home of Anne, Princess Royal, since 1976
Grade II* listed; grounds open occasionally for horse trials and craft fairs

w: Norman lords planted this hilltop town squarely on the Fosse Way to skim trade off every road converging below, and it's been trading ever since - a royal charter has protected its fairs since 1330. A horse fair still sets up on the edge of town each May and October, a rowdy throwback in a genteel market square.
s: A hilltop market town founded to catch passing trade
_facts: Market town on an 800-foot hill at the junction of roads including the Roman Fosse Way
Founded by Norman lords to absorb trade from converging roads
Fairs held by royal charter since 1330
Horse fair still held near Oddington each May and October

w: A mock-medieval folly bristling with turrets and gargoyles, built in the 18th century on Broadway Hill, the second-highest point in the Cotswolds, purely to enjoy the view. It's a genuinely functional building - climb the spiral stair past three museum floors to a rooftop platform on the Cotswold Way.
s: An 18th-century folly on the Cotswolds' second hill
_facts: 18th-century folly tower, Grade II listed, on Broadway Hill
Second-highest point in the Cotswolds at 1,024 feet elevation
Four storeys, hexagonal, with three round corner turrets and battlements
Top three floors used as a museum; rooftop viewing platform
Sits on the Cotswold Way footpath

w: Fugitives from the Battle of Tewkesbury fled into this Norman abbey during the Wars of the Roses, claiming sanctuary - it didn't save them, the pursuing Yorkists dragging them out regardless. What survives is probably the finest Romanesque crossing tower in England, saved by the town buying the building itself.
s: A sanctuary that failed the Wars of the Roses fugitives
_facts: Former Benedictine monastery, now a parish church, in Tewkesbury
One of the finest examples of Norman architecture in Britain, with the largest Romanesque crossing tower in England
Unsuccessfully used as a sanctuary during the Wars of the Roses
Became the parish church after the dissolution of the monasteries
Rings a peal of twelve bells for change ringing

w: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown cut his teeth on this park - his first landscape commission and first architectural job, both done for the 6th Earl of Coventry in the mid-18th century. Robert Adam later touched some interiors. The church in the grounds is kept separately, a folly of faith beside one of landscaping.
_facts: Mid-18th-century Neo-Palladian mansion with landscaped parkland
Designed by Lancelot 'Capability' Brown for George Coventry, 6th Earl of Coventry - Brown's first landscape design and first major architectural project
Some interiors designed by Robert Adam
St Mary Magdalene's Church in the grounds cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust
Parkland owned by the National Trust and open to the public

w: The highest ground in the Cotswolds and in Gloucestershire both, this limestone escarpment looks clean over Cheltenham racecourse to the Severn and Wales beyond, and north across Winchcombe. It's also, oddly, the highest point in the entire Thames drainage basin - common land doing double geographic duty.
s: The Cotswolds' highest point, with a view to Wales
_facts: Highest point of the Cotswold hills and of Gloucestershire, at 330m/1,080ft
Part of Cleeve Common, a Site of Special Scientific Interest
Clear views west to Cheltenham, the Severn and Wales, and north to Winchcombe
Highest point in the drainage basin of the River Thames
Crossed by the Cotswold Way footpath

w: The Great Western Railway built its principal maintenance works here in 1843, and for over a century Swindon's identity was bound up in the sheds where GWR locomotives were built and repaired. The works finally closed in 1986, but the railway town that grew up around them never quite let go of the memory.
s: The GWR works that built the town of Swindon
_facts: Opened by the Great Western Railway in 1843 in Swindon, Wiltshire
Served as the principal west England maintenance centre until closed in 1986

w: Cirencester's Roman incarnation ranked second only to London in sheer footprint - its 2nd-century walls enclosed more ground than any other city in Roman Britain bar the capital. It served as tribal capital of the Dobunni and, later, seat of the province of Britannia Prima itself.
s: A Roman provincial capital under a market town
_facts: Romano-British settlement at Cirencester
2nd-century walls enclosed the second-largest area of any city in Roman Britain
Tribal capital of the Dobunni
Thought to have been capital of the province of Britannia Prima

w: A swineherd's vision of the Virgin Mary supposedly founded this abbey around 700, and by the Middle Ages it had grown into one of the richest in England. Simon de Montfort, killed at the nearby battle in 1265, lies near the old high altar. The dissolution left just a bell tower, a gateway, and fragments.
s: A rich abbey reduced to a bell tower and a grave
_facts: Founded by Saint Egwin around 700-710, following an alleged vision by a swineherd named Eof
Became one of the wealthiest Benedictine abbeys in the country
Simon de Montfort is buried near the site of the high altar, marked with a memorial dedicated in 1965
Dissolution left only a bell tower, gateway, and fragments of the chapter house

w: Retired Roman legionaries were settled here as a colonia in AD 97, the seed that grew into modern Gloucester. Little of Glevum survives to see today, but its name lives on all over the city - in shopfronts, and in the 26-mile Glevum Way footpath tracing the old settlement's edges.
s: The Roman colonia buried beneath modern Gloucester
_facts: Roman fort that became a colonia of retired legionaries in AD 97
Now the site of modern Gloucester
Name survives in local businesses and the 26-mile Glevum Way footpath

w: An Iron Age hillfort with older Bronze Age roots, ringed by double earth banks and a ditch, its innermost rampart once topped with sarsen stone. One of its two original gateways was blocked up not long after construction. It shares its hilltop with the older White Horse carved into the chalk below.
s: An Iron Age hillfort beside the Uffington White Horse
_facts: Early Iron Age hillfort with underlying Bronze Age activity, covering about 3.2 hectares
Surrounded by two earth banks separated by a ditch
One of two original entrances was blocked up a few centuries after construction
Innermost rampart topped with a parapet wall of sarsen stones
Located very close to the Uffington White Horse

w: Cistercian monks founded this abbey in 1246 as a daughter house of Beaulieu, and it thrived until Henry VIII's dissolution wiped it out in 1539. Only low walls and foundations remain today, laid out like a floor plan across the grass, with a small on-site museum holding what artefacts survived.
s: A Cistercian abbey reduced to a grassy floor plan
_facts: Cistercian abbey founded 1246 as a daughter house of Beaulieu Abbey
Dissolved by Henry VIII in 1539
Little remains beyond foundations; Grade I listed scheduled monument
Owned by the National Trust, managed by English Heritage, with an on-site museum

w: Aethelflaed, daughter of Alfred the Great, founded this priory in the 890s as a near-copy of Winchester's Old Minster - a statement of Mercian ambition inside Gloucester's Anglo-Saxon burh walls. It survived as a minor religious house until 1536, then took Civil War damage before being largely pulled down in 1643.
s: A priory founded by Alfred the Great's own daughter
_facts: Founded by Aethelflaed, daughter of Alfred the Great, and her husband Aethelred in the late 880s or 890s
Built as an apparent copy of the Old Minster, Winchester
Supported by the ruling family including King Aethelstan
Declined into a minor house of Canons regular, suppressed in 1536
Damaged in the English Civil War and largely demolished in 1643

w: A Jacobean country house near Moreton-in-Marsh, close in style to the era it was built in and little altered since. The National Trust took over the Grade I listed building in 1991, when its long private ownership finally came to an end.
_facts: Jacobean country house at Chastleton, Oxfordshire, near Moreton-in-Marsh
Owned by the National Trust since 1991
Grade I listed building
